title: Exodus 19:16–25
context: On the third day God descends on Sinai in thunder, lightning, cloud, fire, and a loud trumpet, and the whole mountain quakes. Moses leads the people to the foot of the mountain and goes up when called, and God repeats his warning that neither people nor priests may break through. Both traditions see majesty, holiness, and mediation as shared ground in this awe-filled scene.

verses.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled.
verses.arminianNotes: On the third morning come thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and a very loud trumpet, and the people tremble. Arminian readers see God’s majesty breaking into the ordinary world in overwhelming power. The trembling is a fitting response to holiness, showing that the encounter is real and awe-filled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a theophany that displays God’s glory and terror together. The people’s trembling shows human smallness before the Creator. Both traditions see this scene as a revelation of God’s majesty that frames the law about to be given.

verses.text: Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses leads the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stand at the foot of the mountain. Arminian readers see the people brought near to encounter God, though within the boundaries set. The meeting is purposeful: God has called them to himself, and they come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Moses as mediator leading the people to the appointed meeting place. They approach as far as God permits. Both traditions see an ordered approach, with God’s holiness and his desire for a covenant people held together.

verses.text: All of Mount Sinai smoked, because the LORD descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
verses.arminianNotes: Sinai smokes because the LORD has descended in fire, and the mountain quakes violently. Arminian readers see God’s presence affecting even creation itself. Fire and smoke communicate holiness and power, warning against casual approach while showing the reality of his coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s descent revealing his consuming holiness. The quaking mountain shows creation responding to its Maker. Both traditions see the imagery as communicating majesty and danger, preparing the people to receive his words with reverence.

verses.text: When the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice.
verses.arminianNotes: As the trumpet grows louder, Moses speaks and God answers him with a voice. Arminian readers see a living exchange between God and his servant, witnessed by the people. Revelation is personal communication, not merely spectacle, and Moses’ role as intermediary is confirmed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God answering Moses in a way that authenticates his mediation before Israel. The escalating trumpet heightens the solemnity. Both traditions see the scene fulfilling the earlier promise that the people would hear God speak with Moses.

verses.text: The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. The LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD descends to the summit and calls Moses up. Arminian readers see God drawing his servant into closer communion for the sake of the people. Moses’ ascent marks his unique role, while the people remain below as instructed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD summoning his appointed mediator to the top of the mountain. Access is granted by God’s call, not human initiative. Both traditions see Moses’ privileged position as serving the people rather than elevating himself.

verses.text: The LORD said to Moses, “Go down, warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish.
verses.arminianNotes: God tells Moses to go down and warn the people not to break through to gaze, lest many perish. Arminian readers see God’s protective care even after the boundaries have been set. Repeated warning reflects the real danger of curiosity or presumption before holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s holiness remaining dangerous even to a consecrated people. The warning shows his concern to preserve them. Both traditions note that the passage repeats the boundary to stress how serious it is to approach God on one’s own terms.

verses.text: Let the priests also, who come near to the LORD, sanctify themselves, lest the LORD break out on them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Even the priests who draw near must consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them. Arminian readers see that religious role does not exempt anyone from reverence. Those who approach more closely carry greater responsibility to be prepared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that no one, not even priests, can presume upon nearness to God. Consecration remains necessary for those who serve. Both traditions see a warning that proximity to holy things increases the call to holiness.

verses.text: Moses said to the LORD, “The people can’t come up to Mount Sinai, for you warned us, saying, ‘Set bounds around the mountain, and sanctify it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses replies that the people cannot come up because God has already commanded boundaries. Arminian readers see Moses confident that the instructions have been followed. His answer reflects a real conversation in which the mediator speaks honestly with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Moses recalling God’s own command about the boundaries. The exchange underscores how seriously the instruction is to be kept. Both traditions read the dialogue as showing Moses’ faithfulness and God’s insistence on reverence.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Go down! You shall bring Aaron up with you, but don’t let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them.”
verses.arminianNotes: God tells Moses to go down and return with Aaron, but not to let priests or people break through. Arminian readers see God’s patience in repeating the warning despite Moses’ assurance. The emphasis on Aaron signals his coming role while keeping the people safe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God reaffirming the order of access: Moses and Aaron may come, others must not. Repetition reinforces the danger of presumption. Both traditions see God protecting his people by guarding the boundary he established.

verses.text: So Moses went down to the people, and told them.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses goes down and tells the people. Arminian readers see the mediator faithfully completing his task before the words of the covenant are spoken. The brief verse closes the preparation and leads directly into God’s speaking of the Ten Commandments.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Moses’ obedience as the bridge to the giving of the Decalogue. He delivers the warning as commanded. Both traditions see the narrative now poised for the central revelation of the law in the next chapter.
